text:
🚀 PySpark Optimization Techniques Every Data Engineer Should Know

Working with big data? Performance in PySpark can make or break your pipelines. Here are key optimization techniques used in real-world data engineering 👇

🔹 1. Use Proper Data Formats
✔ Prefer Parquet / ORC over CSV or JSON
✔ Columnar storage = faster reads + compression

🔹 2. Filter Early (Predicate Pushdown)
✔ Apply filter() as early as possible
✔ Reduces data shuffled across the cluster

🔹 3. Avoid Wide Transformations
✔ Minimize groupBy, join, distinct
✔ Use reduceByKey instead of groupByKey

🔹 4. Optimize Joins
✔ Use Broadcast Join for small tables
✔ Tune spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold

🔹 5. Repartition & Coalesce Wisely
✔ repartition() → increase partitions (shuffle)
✔ coalesce() → reduce partitions (no shuffle)

🔹 6. Cache Only When Needed
✔ Use cache() / persist() for reused DataFrames
✔ Unpersist when done to free memory

🔹 7. Avoid UDFs When Possible
✔ Prefer built-in Spark SQL functions
✔ UDFs break query optimization (Catalyst)

🔹 8. Optimize File Size
✔ Avoid too many small files
✔ Target 128MB–1GB per file

🔹 9. Use Explain Plan
✔ df.explain() to analyze physical & logical plans
✔ Spot unnecessary shuffles & scans

📌 Key Takeaway:
Good PySpark performance = less shuffle, fewer scans, smarter joins.

💡 Tools that make life easier:
Spark UI | Databricks | Delta Lake | Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)

From Interview Rejections to Deloitte : My 3 Critical Mistakes (and Fixes)

I failed countless Data Engineer interviews before cracking Deloitte & PwC.

Had the big picture (architecture diagrams ✅), but missed the execution details:

❌ Mistake 1: Weak Fundamentals 
Knew high-level SQL/Python/PySpark, but couldn’t ace basics like: 
`WINDOW functions`, `EXISTS vs IN`, `broadcast joins`, `cache vs persist`
Fix: Daily LeetCode + HackerRank (50+ problems each)

❌ Mistake 2: No Production Mindset 
Talked theory, not reality. Interviewers asked: 
“How do you handle 10TB daily incremental?” 
“What if pipeline fails at 2 AM?” 
“Spark job OOMs - your first 3 steps?”
Fix: Studied real scenarios - cost optimization, retry logic, monitoring

❌ Mistake 3: Ignored Cost Optimization 
Never thought: “How much does this query cost?” 

No clue about partitioning, Z-ordering, cluster sizing

Fix: Azure cost management docs + production pipeline audits

Result? Now at Deloitte building production-grade pipelines with Azure Data Factory, Synapse, & PySpark.

Job Seekers: Don’t make my mistakes! 
Master fundamentals → production scenarios → cost awareness

💡 Pro Tip: For every “architecture” answer, follow with “In production, I’d add X for Y reason”

author: Mranal Sonare
headline: Data & AI at Kyndryl
text:
Recently, I had the opportunity to interview with Wells Fargo for a data-focused role, and one of the SQL questions really stood out.
I was given an orders table with the following columns:
 customer_id, order_date, amount, id (unique row identifier)
The task was to calculate a running total of order amounts for each customer, ordered by order_date and by id when dates were the same.
What made it more interesting?
 I was asked to solve it in two ways:
 - Using window functions
 - Without using window functions

1)Approach 1: Using a Window Function

SELECT
 customer_id,
 order_date,
 amount,
 id,
 SUM(amount) OVER (
 PARTITION BY customer_id
 ORDER BY order_date, id
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
 ) AS running_total
FROM orders;
This solution is clean and efficient.
 The window function allows us to calculate a cumulative total while still keeping each row intact — a very common requirement in analytics and financial data.


2)Approach 2: Without Window Functions

SELECT
 o1.customer_id,
 o1.order_date,
 o1.amount,
 o1.id,
 SUM(o2.amount) AS running_total
FROM orders o1
JOIN orders o2
 ON o1.customer_id = o2.customer_id
 AND (
 o2.order_date < o1.order_date
 OR (o2.order_date = o1.order_date AND o2.id <= o1.id)
 )
GROUP BY
 o1.customer_id, o1.order_date, o1.amount, o1.id
ORDER BY
 o1.customer_id, o1.order_date, o1.id;


Here, the running total is built by joining each order with all previous orders from the same customer. It’s more computationally heavy, but it shows a deeper understanding of how cumulative logic works under the hood.

- Key Takeaways from This Question
Window functions are powerful for row-level analytics
But strong SQL skills mean knowing how to solve problems even without advanced features
Handling ordering edge cases (like ties on dates) is critical
Interviewers often test thinking and approach, not just syntax
Grateful for experiences that push me to think beyond basic queries and strengthen my fundamentals.
Back to sharpening SQL every day.

author: Fayyaz Ahmed Bepari
headline: Data architect.
text:
SQL QUERY OPTIMIZATION techniques every data engineer must know 


1 Use Indexes Smartly

Indexes shine on high-cardinality columns. Don't index everything - it slows writes.

2 Avoid SELECT*

Selecting only required columns reduces scan time + network I/O.

3 Use EXISTS instead of IN (for large subqueries)

EXISTS stops after the first match → usually faster.

4 Optimize JOINs using indexed keys Joining on unindexed columns is one of the biggest performance killers.

5 Filter Early (WHERE before GROUP BY/HAVING) Shrinking the dataset early = faster computation later.

6 Avoid functions on indexed columns

WHERE DATE(timestamp) blocks index usage completely.

7 Prefer UNION ALL instead of UNION

UNION = deduplication = expensive sorting.

8 Don't do wildcard-leading searches

LIKE '%text'→ full scan.

LIKE 'text%' → index friendly.

9 Partition large tables Especially for time-series data; improves pruning dramatically.

10 Always check the query plan (EXPLAIN) Most engineers don't - but this shows WHERE the bottleneck really is.
